papers.title: Crucible: Evaluating LLM Agents in Executable Chemistry Research Environments
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform well on chemistry knowledge benchmarks, which mainly assess question answering and isolated tasks. Chemical research, however, requires using specialized tools and interpreting their outputs to obtain chemically valid results. To address this gap, we introduce Crucible Bench to evaluate this ability across all four stages of the design-make-test-analyze (DMTA) cycle. The benchmark contains 1,078 tasks in 12 task families curated from 18 published datasets, covering molecular design, synthesis planning, experimental execution, closed-loop optimization, simulation, and analytical characterization. Agents access 75 domain-specific tools through the Model Context Protocol in seven isolated environments. Sandboxed graders verify the resulting synthesis routes, experimental protocols, and other outputs. Laboratory tasks use robotic simulators or previously measured experimental data. We evaluate 14 LLMs as agents and find that the best achieves an overall score of 0.545, with synthesis planning and closed-loop optimization emerging as the hardest domains. Overall performance does not predict optimization performance well: the model ranked twelfth overall achieves the highest score in closed-loop optimization. Error analysis also shows that agents often submit chemically invalid results despite running their tools successfully. Stronger models benefit more from tool access, but reliable use of chemical software remains a challenge that Crucible Bench can track as models improve.

papers.title: DLaR: Dynamic Stochasticity Control for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Latent reasoning enables LLMs to operate in continuous embedding space, yet existing methods suffer from deterministic inference that precludes exploration of diverse reasoning paths. While recent approaches inject stochasticity to restore exploration, we identify two fundamental limitations: \textit{uniform stochasticity} across all steps is suboptimal, and unconstrained perturbations disrupt reasoning coherence. We propose Dynamic Stochasticity Control for Latent Reasoning (DLaR), a framework with two complementary mechanisms that operate at different temporal granularities within the GRPO reinforcement learning framework. At the token level, Adaptive Stochasticity Modulation (ASM) dynamically adjusts perturbation intensity at each latent step based on a confidence-entropy fusion signal, increasing exploration when the model is uncertain and preserving stability when confident. At the training level, Training-Aware Stochasticity Tuning (TAST) progressively decays the base stochasticity level following a curriculum schedule. Through this dual-level design, DLaR establishes a hierarchical exploration-exploitation strategy that operates at both token and training levels. Extensive experiments on four in-distribution and three out-of-distribution mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that DLaR achieves the highest average performance across model scales, reaching 27.9%/50.6% Pass@1/Pass@8 on Llama-3.2-1B and 46.8%/68.2% on Qwen2.5-1.5B. Code: \href{https://github.com/xiaocen-luo/DLaR}{https://github.com/xiaocen-luo/DLaR}.

papers.title: ZeroHero: Training Small Language Agents from Scratch
papers.abstract: Large pretrained language models provide capable policies for interactive tasks, but how much model capacity is necessary for a specialized language agent? We introduce ZeroHero, a framework for training small language agents (SLAs) from scratch. In each environment, a large language model acts as the expert, and we collect its successful trajectories. We pretrain each SLA, which has fewer than 50 million parameters, to predict the expert's responses given the interaction history. We then post-train the agent on its own interactions using proximal policy optimization (PPO). During post-training, reasoning alignment supplements environment rewards with expert supervision on the language the agent generates alongside its actions. We evaluate the agents in three multistep environments where acting requires both understanding and generating language. In Crafter, agents interpret textual observations and generate reasoning before acting. In WebShop, they translate shopping instructions into search queries. In Alfworld-Dialogue, they ask clarifying questions and use the answers to guide household actions. The agents approach expert performance on WebShop and surpass their respective demonstration experts on Crafter training rollouts and held-out Alfworld-Dialogue tasks. An interactive demo is available at https://zoyav.github.io/-ZoyaV-zerohero-demo.

papers.title: EvoLink-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Self-Evolving Agents in Long-Horizon Interdependent Task Streams
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from passive chatbots into autonomous systems that operate continuously in dynamic environments. Such agents need not only solve current tasks but also learn from past interactions to improve future performance. However, existing streaming benchmarks often rely on short task sequences or largely independent tasks, providing limited evidence of whether agents can effectively reuse experience when later tasks depend on earlier outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{EvoLink-Bench}, a benchmark for evaluating self-evolving agents in long-horizon, interdependent task streams. It covers daily office work, multi-turn dialogue, and AutoResearch-style workflows, with persistent workspaces and dependencies across tasks. The benchmark includes two complementary levels: \textbf{L1}, which evaluates the acquisition and revision of language-expressible knowledge, and \textbf{L2}, which assesses the development of task-level capabilities through execution and feedback. Its evaluation further distinguishes within-task recovery, persistent-state updates, and experience reuse in later tasks. We evaluate five agent frameworks across three backbone configurations under three persistence conditions, covering 19,635 scored task slots from selected evaluation cohorts. Results show that no framework consistently performs best across both levels, retries recover only a limited proportion of failed tasks, and persistent-state updates do not necessarily improve subsequent performance. Furthermore, the effects of evolution differ between knowledge- and capability-level tasks, suggesting that these two forms of evolution require different learning mechanisms. Performance gains also vary across domains and task streams, with improvements on some tasks not necessarily extending to others.

papers.title: Disturbances and climate drive tree elevational shifts
papers.abstract: Abstract Climate change and disturbances are reshaping forest ecosystems worldwide 1–4 , yet their combined effects on species redistribution remain poorly understood. Here we analyse repeated measurements from 44,368 forest inventory plots spanning 1999–2025, with an average remeasurement interval of 10 years, to examine how climate and natural disturbances jointly influence the elevational redistribution of tree species across the western USA. We show that climate warming increased sapling abundance, whereas increasing drought frequency and recent natural disturbances (fire, insect outbreaks and disease) reduced tree abundance, particularly among adult trees. By contrast, legacy fire was associated with increased sapling abundance, with stronger positive responses in angiosperms than in gymnosperms. These influences were distributed unevenly across species’ elevational ranges: upper portions of species’ ranges generally experienced stronger warming, greater increases in drought frequency and more disturbance activity than lower portions, creating elevational asymmetries in stress and recovery. These elevational asymmetries were associated with more pronounced downslope shifts in basal area centres, probably reflecting disturbance effects on larger trees. By contrast, stem abundance centres showed more divergent shifts, consistent with sapling responses to both climate change and disturbance. Our findings reveal contrasting demographic responses to climate change and natural disturbances that shape the elevational redistribution of different species, with potential consequences for forest composition, resilience and long-term stability.

papers.title: Transcription from megabase-scale heterochromatin generates neural barcodes
papers.abstract: Abstract Heterochromatin typically represses genes 1,2 , yet some genes paradoxically require it for activation 3–7 . How can the same chromatin environment both silence and promote transcription? Here we address this question by interrogating the clustered protocadherin (Pcdh) locus, where subsets of genes are stochastically expressed while most remain silent 8 . In neurons, stochastic and combinatorial expression of Pcdh genes generates unique cell-surface barcodes required for self–non-self discrimination and neural circuit assembly 8 . By combining RNA labelling of Pcdh genes and neurodevelopmental cell types with single-molecule chromatin tracing and stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy, we find that a compact heterochromatin domain containing Pcdh genes forms as these genes become activated during development. Pcdh transcription occurs within the compact domain and reads through downstream genes, and distal enhancers must access the domain to engage target promoters. Genetic perturbations in mice suggest that opposing genome folding forces cooperate to establish Pcdh locus architecture and promote stochastic Pcdh expression. Specifically, while DNA loop extrusion allows enhancers to breach heterochromatin and find target promoters, heterochromatin-driven compartmentalization supports an expanded enhancer–promoter search space. These findings shed light on a process foundational to the development of vertebrate nervous systems and suggest a mechanism for how transcription can occur within seemingly silent chromatin environments.

papers.title: A thalamo-amygdalar circuit drives female vulnerability to chronic pain after early-life stress
papers.abstract: Childhood adversity increases the risk of chronic pain and anxiety later in life, particularly in women, yet the neural mechanisms linking early-life stress to adult vulnerability remain elusive. Here, we show that social isolation and nerve injury interact to amplify activity-dependent synaptic gain and anticipatory recruitment of the paraventricular thalamus-to–central amygdala pathway in female, but not male, mice. This female-specific circuit sensitization enhances mechanical hypersensitivity and avoidance behaviors in adulthood. Chemogenetic pathway inhibition selectively rescued these behaviors when stress and injury co-occurred, whereas sustained and phasic pathway activation triggered mechanical hypersensitivity and avoidance, respectively. Together, these findings uncovered a latent thalamo-amygdalar synaptic gain state that is unmasked by a subsequent injury and transforms early-life stress into female-specific vulnerability to chronic pain and anxiety-like avoidance.

papers.title: Elastic-field reorganization stabilizes soft-lattice perovskites for durable solar cells
papers.abstract: The soft lattice that enables the exceptional performance of halide perovskites inherently compromises their operational stability. Here, we show that soft-lattice perovskites can be stabilized through elastic-field reorganization induced by rigid nanodiamond inclusions. Their inclusion enabled efficient bulk-to-boundary load transfer, redistributing and dissipating internal elastic fields at grain boundaries rather than allowing their accumulation within the crystal interior. Suppression of intergranular sliding constrained lattice deformation and mitigated defect generation during prolonged operation. Devices based on the stabilized perovskites with an area of 0.09 square centimeters achieved a certified power conversion efficiency of 27.6%, and minimodules with an area of 16.1 square centimeters achieved 24.3%. These devices retained 80% of their initial PCE after 5000 hours of maximum power point operation at 85°C and 98% after 5000 hours of dynamically varying light-intensity day-night cycling.
